s06a.slug: FRIDAY · 6:30 PM · I-10 EAST, PICACHO → MARANA — ONE SENTENCE
body: Lena was in the way-back before anybody else had a door open, the legal pad shut on her pen. Now Margot has the wheel, both hands on it where the driver’s manual puts them, the needle laid on sixty-five and kept there. Kevin rides shotgun with the map light on and Pinal County open on his knee. Theo has come back to the middle-left beside Jack with his camel coat folded across his lap, and Laney is in the way-back behind Jack, and Lena is behind Theo, in the corner of the van farthest from anything.

Behind them the peak has gone flat black against a sky that is still orange along the bottom and navy everywhere else. The saguaros along the right-of-way go dark against it, every one of them with its arms up, and the orange thins to a line along the mountains, and then the line goes, and it’s the dashboard and the road and the red lights of a cattle truck far ahead. The van hasn’t said a word since the pump. The tires have, and the fan in the dash, and once Kevin, turning a page of Arizona under the little light: “Marana.” Its lights come up ahead out of the flat, low and yellow: a truck stop, a water tower, a long lit fence around something agricultural.

The call is still on him. He can feel where the RAZR was warm against his ear, and he has her laugh, the real one, with the trailer’s space heater going behind it in Burnaby, and *Bye, Pair Forty-one*, which he’s still turning over. Up front Theo’s iPod sits dark in the cup holder with its transmitter. Behind Jack, Laney’s BlackBerry throws a little light up onto the ceiling, and goes out, and comes on again. The book is in his lap with his hand on it.
From the way-back, to her own window, Lena says, “You always did read a margin well.”

It isn’t loud. It doesn’t have to be. There’s no Kevin in it and no Laney: nine days since Hale’s, and the first sentence she has put in the air for him comes straight across the van with nobody’s name on the envelope, and there’s no question in the car whose it is. Kevin’s hand stops on the map light. Behind Jack, Laney’s head comes up off the window. Beside him Theo shuts his eyes, the way a man shuts them on a plane when the wheels come up.

Jack hears the pump in it: Hale’s pencil, and his own voice going across the island to a trailer in Burnaby while five people checked tire pressure they had already checked. That’s what she means. She has sat on it since the Picacho exit, and she has picked her moment, and her moment is now.

choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You told her Skye asked.
response: “She asked,” he says, over his left shoulder.
“She asks for a lot,” Lena says, to the glass.
Marana comes up level with them and starts to go by on the right, the truck stop and the tower and the long lit fence, and none of it is any help. He turns around the rest of the way.

choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You told Kevin to tell her thank you. Kevin said no.
response: “Kevin,” he says. “Tell her thank you.”
Kevin doesn’t turn around. His hand is still up on the map light, and he says it to the windshield, perfectly pleasant, the first relay he has turned down since the Rincon. “No.”
“He’s not a switchboard, Costigan,” Lena says. “He said so.”
So it’s Costigan, then, out loud, in the van, with Marana going by. Jack turns around in his seat to have a look at her.

choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You said nothing. She went on anyway.
response: He says nothing. He watches Marana come up out of the dark on the right and lets her have the window.
She doesn’t need him. “It’s a talent,” she says, in the same tone, conversational, a woman remarking on the scenery. “You should do it for everybody. I hear you do.”
And his head comes around, all on its own, over his left shoulder.

choices.key: Past Picacho Lena spoke to you for the first time since Hale’s: you always did read a margin well. You said: you’d know.
response: “You’d know,” he says.
He hears it go in. He doesn’t have to turn around to hear it. Behind Theo the way-back goes still, a room with a glass gone over at the far end of it.
She lets it lie there while Marana’s lights go by, the truck stop and the tower and the long fence sliding back past her window. When the dark has the van again she starts, and she has plenty.

s07.slug: FRIDAY · 7:00 PM · I-10 EAST, TUCSON — THE CAPTION
body: Tucson is a grid of lights laid flat on both sides of the interstate, streetlights running off in dead-straight lines toward mountains that are only a darker part of the dark now, the Catalinas, with a red light blinking on a tower somewhere along the top. Margot holds sixty-five through all of it. To fight in this van Jack has to turn in his seat over his left shoulder and talk past the side of Theo’s headrest to the corner of the way-back, with the shoulder belt sawing at his collarbone, and that is how he fights it.
“Some of us got our margins read to us too,” Lena says. “I didn’t know it was a *repertoire*.”
“It’s a book, Broussard.”

“It’s a *bit*. It’s a bit you do.” In the light off the cattle truck they’re passing he can see her sitting very straight, the legal pad face-down on her knees, both hands flat on it. “And she’s so good at bits. *We agree on each other.*” She reads him the caption in no voice at all, the way you’d read the side of a cereal box. “*Not just friends from school.* And the little heart. Less than three. She did the arithmetic for four hundred people.”

body.text: “And then you made it your *face*. And she wrote under it, for everybody: *happy looks good on you.*” The same no voice, every word of it, like she’s read it more than once.

body: “She can’t have a sandwich,” Lena says, “without telling four hundred people.”
Behind him Laney says, low, “Lena.”
“I’m talking about the *weather*, Laney. I’m making conversation with the man. We’ve got nineteen hundred miles.”

“You want the caption?” He’s round as far as the belt lets him. “I’ll give you the caption. They had me in a room full of people who’d paid to be there for a senator from a state I can’t vote in and wouldn’t if I could, with the senator’s name on a banner over the stairs and a man with a camera at the bottom of them. She didn’t walk me out. She could have. She stood me up in the middle of it and asked every one of them why they thought I was wrong, and then she shut up and let me answer, one after another, all night, in a room that was supposed to be theirs. And when they wanted the picture at the end, me under the banner, she wouldn’t give it to them. She took a picture of tacos. So nobody back home opens a paper and thinks I stood for something I don’t.” He hears his voice go up the inside of the van and doesn’t bring it down. “That’s what she posted. That’s your sandwich.”
“So she *edited* you,” Lena says.
“She *argued* me. In a room that paid to watch me lose. You know the difference. You’ve got her caption by heart, you can work it out.”

“It’s a *caption*, Costigan. I’ve got the Exsultet by heart, and it runs a good deal longer, and nobody’s made me a deacon.” She doesn’t let him have the laugh, if there was one in it. “If it was real, why put it up? Real keeps. You don’t have to tell four hundred people about a thing that’s real. It’ll still be there in the morning.”

“Because somebody else was going to put up the other one. That’s how it goes when people have been taking your picture since you were a kid. You get there first, or you get the one they pick.” He has the seat back in his fist. “They built her that window, Lena. She didn’t. And you’ve got your face pressed up against it every night, reading the comments.”
“I don’t have to read the comments. I hear them in the Fishbowl. You’re *Mystery Guy*, Costigan. You’ve got a following. Doug Pruitt says it across the Commons like it’s your name.”
“I didn’t ask to be anybody’s mystery.”
“No. You just stood where the camera was.”

body.text: “You don’t care,” Lena says. “You said so. Loud enough for the hatch.” She waits. “Not unless it’s got a caption on it.”
“You’re not a subscriber,” Lena says. “You said so. Loud enough for the hatch.” She waits. “Not unless it’s got a caption on it.”
“You don’t care,” Lena says. “You asked her why she’d think you would. Loud enough for the hatch.” She waits. “Not unless it’s got a caption on it.”

body: “That one,” Jack says, “I meant.”
“Good,” Lena says. “Then we agree on something. Write it on a napkin. She’ll post it.”

In the middle-left Theo has turned his face to his window as though there were something out there in the dark besides Tucson’s last car dealerships going by, and behind Jack, Laney has taken her sunglasses off her head and put them on, at seven at night, in a van.
Up front Kevin turns round in his seat with Arizona slipping off his knee. “Respectfully, could we —”
“*No*,” say Jack and Lena.

Kevin faces front. He reaches up and switches off the map light, and keeps his hand on it a little while in the dark, and then takes the hand down and leaves the light off, and sits there with Pima County on his knee where he can’t read it.

choices.text: “She posted tacos so a fundraiser couldn’t use me. You want to tell me what’s fake about that?”
response: “Tell me what’s fake about it. Go ahead. She posted tacos so a fundraiser couldn’t use me.”

“Nothing,” Lena says. “Nothing in the world. It’s the most sincere marketing I’ve ever seen.” She tips her head at him in the dark. “She marketed *you*, Costigan. To you. And look at you. You bought it twice.”

choices.text: “You’ve been keeping up with her page, then.”
response: “You’ve kept up with her page, then. Good to know somebody reads it.”

“Everybody keeps up with her page, Costigan. That’s what a page is *for*.” She doesn’t miss a stride. “A diary, you have to steal out of a drawer. She leaves hers out on the porch with the lights on.”

choices.text: “Fine. She posts. She’s posted since she was a kid. For years the network did it for her.”
response: “Fine. She posts. She’s posted since she was a kid. For years the network did it for her, and she didn’t get a vote.”

It stops her. He watches it stop her, in the corner of the way-back, her mouth closing on whatever she had ready next. It doesn’t last. “Then she’s had a lot of practice,” Lena says, and it comes back harder for the stop, and he is sorry he gave her anything.

choices.text: “You read the rest of the screen in the lounge. I watched you shut the laptop.”
response: “You read the rest of the screen in the lounge,” he says. “I was in the door. I watched you shut the laptop.”
The way-back goes silent, with nothing in the silence at all. When she speaks it’s level. “I shut it because Laney had crumbs in the keyboard.”
“I did *not*,” Laney says.
It’s the cruelest thing he has said to her tonight, and he knows it because it worked.

s08.slug: FRIDAY · 8:10 PM · I-10 EAST, TEXAS CANYON — WORD FOR WORD
body: Texas Canyon comes up in the headlights all at once, in Arizona, where nobody asked it to: boulders, round and gray, heaped on both sides of the road taller than the van, one balanced on another balanced on a third, as if something enormous had set them down in piles and forgotten to come back for them. The lights sweep them and let them go, and they’re gone behind.

“You’re still telling it wrong,” Lena says. “To everybody. Kenzie Rourke stopped me outside the Fishbowl on Tuesday to tell me she’s on my *side*.” Lena says *side* as if Kenzie had handed it to her wet. “I don’t want a side. I want it to have happened the way it happened.”
“Doug Pruitt asked me Monday if you threw a jam jar at Hale’s dog.”
“I did not throw a —”
“I know. I told him you threw it at me.”
“Well, that’s the one he tells now. Thank you. I’m a *menace* in the Classics department.”
Margot’s eyes come up to the mirror and go back to the road.

body.text: “There are eight versions of me calling you a liar, Lena,” Jack says, “and in seven of them I’m right.”
body.else: “There are eight versions of Wednesday, Lena,” Jack says, “and in seven of them I’m right.”

body: “Then say it right.”
“I can do it word for word.”
“So can I.”

And they do. Both of them, at the same moment, every line of it, hers and his, in two voices over the road noise, her Louisiana and his Ohio laid one on top of the other like two parishes saying the Creed:
“Will you be around after? Monday night. Nine, ten.”
“Probably not. I’ve got a thing.”
“Okay. Then call me after. Eat something first.”
“I haven’t been fair to him, Jack. I’ve known it a while. I’m going to fix it.”

body.text: “He’s a good guy, Lena. He deserves that.”
“Fix it how? Write him a song?”

body: It comes out even. The same words in the same order, down to the *and*s, and when it’s over the van has gone so quiet under it that the fan in the dash sounds loud.
Margot, driving, to nobody: “Those were the same words.”
“Then you know what I said,” Lena says.
“I know exactly what you said.”
“So tell them what it meant,” Lena says. “Go on. Tell the van.”
“You tell them. It was your call.”
The van waits. Margot drives. Neither of them tells anybody anything.
“You *know* —” She stops. Whatever was behind it she puts back. “Who taught you to do it so pretty? You had it by heart. You had the *pauses*.”
“I said it word for word to one person,” Jack says, “once, and that was Theo. Because he asked me to.”
“*Laney* made me do it,” Lena says. “Twice. At the *mailboxes*.”
His head comes round to the left, to Theo, at the same moment hers comes round to the right, to Laney.
“Anthropology,” says Theo, to the back of Kevin’s seat.
“Sugar,” Laney says, “I was making *conversation*.”
Margot keeps her eyes on the road. “I’ve asked nobody anything. I’d like that minuted.”
“I said leave it alone,” Kevin says, without turning around. “In January.”

Margot takes one hand off the wheel, which Jack has not seen her do since Picacho, and drives a mile of Cochise County that way while she rubs her eyes under her glasses with the other. “I should have taken the train,” she tells the windshield.
From the way-back, to nobody, in a very small voice, Laney says, “We could play Two Truths.” Two Truths does not get played.

It doesn’t last, whatever it was, because Lena has worked it out the other way. Jack can see her get there; he gets there with her. If Theo had to ask, Theo had a reason to. If Laney made her do it twice —
“What did you tell him it *was*?” she says.
“What did you tell *her*?”
“You told Theo I —”
“You told Laney I —”
And there it stops, his and hers, at the word neither one will say in this car.

body.text: “You’re a liar, Costigan,” Lena says. Not at a table this time. Close, in the dark, with nowhere for anybody to go. “And now there are witnesses who were *told*.”
body.else: “Then one of us is lying to a best friend,” Lena says, close, in the dark, with nowhere for anybody to go, “and I know which.”

body: “Twice,” Jack says. “At the mailboxes. You needed two takes, Lena? For *Laney*?”
“And Theo got it the first time.” She doesn’t look at Theo; she doesn’t have to. “Theo gets everything the first time, if you say it tired enough and look at the floor.”
Beside Jack, Theo looks at the floor.

choices.text: “Same words. Every one. You want them again?”
response: “Same words. Every one. You want them again? I’ll do yours this time. I’ve got your part.”
“Once was plenty,” Lena says. “I was there for the first one.”

choices.text: “Two people heard the same call. Maybe nobody’s lying. Maybe —”
response: “Two people heard the same call,” he says. “Maybe nobody’s lying. Maybe —”

“Don’t you *dare* be reasonable at me in a car.” She’s on top of it before he gets to the end, and she doesn’t let him have the end. But a rest area goes by on the right with its lights on, and in the light her face says she heard the half he got out.

choices.text: “Laney took notes? Did she bring them? Laney, did you bring the notes?”
response: He turns the other way, to the seat behind his. “Laney took notes? Did she bring them? Laney. Did you bring the notes?”
“I will put you out of this car,” Laney says, “at seventy miles an hour.”
“Sixty-five,” says Kevin, from the front.
Lena hasn’t laughed. Lena is waiting for him to come back round to her, and when he does she is right where he left her.

choices.text: “You lied to your best friend so she’d hate me. It worked. Look at her.”
response: “You lied to your best friend so she’d hate me,” he says. “It worked. Look at her.”
Behind him, very quietly, close to his ear: “Don’t you put me in it, fireman.”
Lena doesn’t answer. She goes quiet for longer than she has been quiet since Picacho, long enough that he thinks he’s won something, and then she starts again on new ground, which is worse.

s09.slug: FRIDAY · 8:55 PM · I-10 EAST, THE NEW MEXICO LINE — CERTIFICATION
body: WELCOME TO NEW MEXICO comes up white in the headlights and goes by on the right, and they are in another state, and the state looks exactly like the last one: flat, black, a fence line, the far red lights of the trucks ahead.

Theo leans forward between the front seats and turns the radio on. It finds a sports station out of Tucson, still hanging on, and a man who is very sure about tendons: Freeney’s ankle, what the Colts are saying about it, what the Colts aren’t. The man has a lot of it. Margot reaches over without taking her eyes off the road and turns him off.
“I am going to be sick,” Laney says, behind Jack. “I mean it.” She doesn’t mean the road.
Kevin reaches back between the seats without turning around and holds out a plastic Safeway bag from the first-aid kit, folded square. Laney takes it and holds it in her lap with both hands.
Hale’s copy is on Jack’s knee, where it has been since Picacho, his hand flat on the cover. Lena looks at it in the dash light across Theo’s lap. She looks at him.

“You know what Binx calls it,” she says. “In that book. When he goes to the movies and there’s his own neighborhood up on the screen, his own street, and he walks out and all of a sudden it’s a real place to him. He’s *certified*.” She knows it cold; she doesn’t reach for a page. “That’s her, Jack. Nothing has happened to that girl until somebody’s seen it. The airport. The Walk. The singalong. The tacos. A parking lot at a quarter to five with a priest in it. Certified, every one. It isn’t real till it’s in the movie.”

“That’s backward.” He’s got the book up off his knee, and his thumb finds the corner of the print where it lies in the pages, face-down, and stays there. “Percy’s whole point is that’s the *sickness*. That’s what’s wrong with Binx. The man who has to see his street in a movie to believe he lives on it is the sick one, Broussard. That’s the joke. That’s the book.”
“I know the book.”
“Then read it.”
“I read it on the seawall at the lakefront when I was sixteen, Costigan. It’s my city in it. Binx lives in Gentilly. I could walk you to his street.”
“Then you know what he does all day. He sits in the dark and watches other people be alive. That’s the sick part. Not the people on the screen. Him.”
“Exactly,” Lena says. “So who’s in the seat, Jack? Who’s sitting in the dark watching her be alive?”
It goes in. He feels it go in, and he gives her nothing on his face, and she watches him give her nothing.
She lets Percy go. She reaches for the lot.

“She hit her mark, Jack,” Lena says. “Father Osei said *stand*, and she asked him for her blocking. I heard her across the hood. And she found her light.” Her voice doesn’t go up; it goes careful, precise, a woman reading back a list. “The circle at a quarter to five. The eyes shut, the head down, beautiful. The water on the back of her hand, and she held it up and looked at it like she was checking it for her close-up. The Walk in your flannel.”

body.text: “Candlemas, with a candle. She held your candle so you could sit.”

body: “She’s wearing it,” Lena says. “All of it. Like wardrobe. The candle and the water and the circle, every bit of it a costume she’ll give back when she’s done with it, and you hand it to her. You *dress* her in it.” Her pen is in her fist. “You think you’re being respectful. That’s not respect. That’s blocking.”
There is a thing that happens to the inside of a car when somebody says something like that in it. He feels it go round the van and come back and land on him.

“She has not pretended to believe one single thing she doesn’t,” he says, and it is louder than Tucson, louder than anything he has said tonight, loud enough that Kevin’s shoulders come up. “Not to me. Not to Osei. Not to you. She came to Mass with me and asked me after to explain it, properly, start to finish, and listened to every word of the answer. She walked the Walk and argued every sign on it fair and didn’t make fun of one. She stood because a priest asked her to stand. She shut her eyes because that’s what you do when somebody’s praying for you. That’s called *manners*, Lena. They’ve got it in Louisiana. She stood in a circle in a parking lot at a quarter to five, with a plane to catch, and let a man throw water on her, and said *amen* to it.” He’s run out of breath and found more. “That’s more than you’ve done for her.”

“For *her*?” Lena says. “Lord have mercy. I told her safe flight. To her face, across a hood, at a quarter to five in the morning. I meant it.” She pulls the hood of her sweatshirt down off her head as if it had gotten hot in there. “I hope it was. I hope she had the window.”

choices.text: “Percy’s on my side. Binx gets better when he quits watching. You’re the one keeping the tape.”
response: “Percy’s on my side,” he says. “Binx gets better when he quits watching. She quit. You’re the one keeping the tape.”
“Binx gets better when he gets *married*, Costigan,” Lena says. “Read to the end.”
It lands in the van like a tray dropped in a cafeteria, and then everybody pretends very hard not to have heard it fall, and Lena goes on looking at him, and he goes on looking back.

choices.text: “She does like an audience. She grew up in front of one. That isn’t the same as lying.”
response: “She likes an audience,” he says. “Okay. She grew up in front of one. That isn’t the same as lying.”

Lena is quiet long enough for a sign to go by, mileage to Lordsburg. “No,” she says. “It isn’t.” And then, harder, because he handed her that and she can see what to do with it: “It’s worse. Liars know.”
“You’d know about wardrobe,” he says. “You veil.”

“I veil for God, Costigan.” Not a half-second’s gap. “He doesn’t have a Facebook.” Her pen comes down on the legal pad in her lap. “Mine’s black lace, and I bought it with my own money, and there is not one picture of me in it anywhere on God’s earth, and there isn’t going to be.”

choices.text: “You don’t know what she came out of. Her mother —”
response: “You don’t know what she came out of,” he says. “Her mother —”

It’s right there in his mouth, the next word and the ones after it, and every one of them would win. He stops on the second word, and the van hears him stop, the way you hear a door shut somewhere in a house when you never saw it open.
“Her mother what?” Lena says.
“Nothing. It’s not mine.”
Lena looks at him for a long count across Theo, and then she goes formal on him, every vowel in its place. “Of course it isn’t,” she says, very politely, and he would rather she had hit him.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 9:20 PM · I-10 EAST, LORDSBURG — PERFORMING
body: Lordsburg is a few lights on the left: a motel sign with two letters out, a truck stop’s tall pole sign lit yellow, a drive-in shut for the night. Up front Kevin leans across to read the gauge past Margot’s arm.
“Respectfully,” Kevin says, “we’re at half. Lordsburg has a —”
“There’s nowhere to stop,” Margot says.
“There’s a *sign* for it.”
“This is the Chihuahuan Desert.”

She doesn’t take the exit. The truck-stop sign comes level with them, yellow, enormous, and slides back over Kevin’s shoulder and into the dark, and Kevin watches it go in the side mirror like a man watching his ride leave the curb. Margot’s knuckles on the wheel are white.

Behind Jack, Laney reaches over in the way-back and puts her hand on Lena’s wrist. Lena takes the wrist back. Laney’s hand stays out a moment in the dark, and then it comes and takes hold of the back of Jack’s seat, by his shoulder, and grips there, and doesn’t let go of it again.
“She plays the good girl for money,” Lena says, “and the bad girl for free.”
He has been turned round in this seat since Tucson. The belt has worn a line into the side of his neck and he can’t feel it.

“Thursdays at nine she’s Cassidy,” Lena says. “The nice one. Everybody’s little sister. That’s the job, and they pay her for it, and good for her. And the rest of the week she gives the other one away to anybody with a phone. The airport. The Walk on a website, with question marks after it. The singalong.” She has them all lined up, the way she had the call. “She didn’t put that one up. She didn’t have to. A stranger did it for her, which is the best kind of publicity there is. And then she wrote on *your* wall. *For everybody watching at home.*”

“It’s a *job*,” he says. “She’s good at it. They don’t hand those out. My nonna watches her every Thursday night on Glenwood Avenue and prays for her by the wrong name, and she doesn’t care which name, and God doesn’t seem to mind either.”
“Your *grandmother*,” Lena says. It stops her for the length of a reflector post going by in the lights, and then she steps over it.

body.text: “You wanted the hood,” she says. “You should’ve taken it.”
“And you kissed her like nobody was in the lot. Six of us were in the lot. One of us was a *priest*.”
“And you promised her a doubloon. In front of a *priest*.”
“And you’re going to call her at the *kickoff*. Who calls at a *kickoff*?”
“— and the two of you getting out of that Saab at a quarter to five like it was a *premiere*.”

body: “You were in the lot,” he says. “You had a seat for all of it. You didn’t have to watch. You watched every second, and now you want to tell me who the audience was.”
“I was standing *in* it, Costigan. Across the hood from her. I could see her count.”

“You want to talk about an audience?” He doesn’t know where his hands are until he finds one of them gripping the headrest beside Theo’s ear. “You’ve had one since the Rincon. Fourteen hours of a temperature and a window and *Kevin, tell him*. That’s a two-hander, Lena. You wrote it. You cast Kevin. You’ve been doing it at me across three states for an audience of four who can’t get out of the car, and you want to talk to me about a *stage*?”
“Costigan,” Theo says, beside him.

It comes in with the road noise, part of the car. Theo has his elbows on his knees and his face in his hands, the camel coat slid off onto the floor between his shoes, and nothing is coming out of him, no pitch, no title, nothing about a picture anybody would want to make of this.

Lena doesn’t answer the stage. She goes around it. “You told a table full of people you come in the side door at Mass so nobody has to look at you. And then you stand in a circle in a parking lot next to her with a priest, so everybody can.”
“And today,” Lena says. “A margin. For an audience of five. At a *gas station*.”

body.text: Before the next word she falters. Half a second: her breath catches on nothing, and for that half second in the dash light she looks eighteen. He sees it. It makes him angrier.
She has run out of book. Somewhere back by the state line she stopped arguing Percy with him, and what she goes to now is the girl herself.
She goes straight through it without a pause, as she came through Tucson and the canyon and the state line, and doesn’t slow down for any of it.

body: “She’s performing *again*,” Lena says, “and you’re standing there holding the book for her.”

choices.key: Past Lordsburg Lena said Skye was performing again. You took the word apart, and then you said the thing about a movie called *Jack*.
response: “*Performing*,” he says, and takes it apart in front of her, piece by piece, with the van listening. She stood up in a circle because a priest asked. She shut her eyes because somebody was praying over her. She put up tacos so a man with a camera wouldn’t get his picture. She asked him to read to her down a phone at a gas pump because she’d been up since four and was a long way from anybody she knew. Every one a thing done for somebody else. He lays them out across the van like tools on a tailgate and she sits there and lets him and doesn’t pick up a single one.
He opens his mouth.

choices.key: Past Lordsburg Lena said Skye was performing again. You dared her to say it again. She did, and then you said the thing about a movie called *Jack*.
response: “Say it again,” he says. “Go ahead. Say *performing* again.”
She does. She says it slowly, every syllable of it, looking straight at him across Theo’s bowed head: “Per-*form*-ing. *Again*.”
He opens his mouth.

choices.text: “Maybe she is. At least she does it where I can see it.”

response: “Maybe she is,” he says. “Maybe she is. At least she does it where I can see it.”
It isn’t a concession, and he knows it while it’s still coming out of him.
“Where you can *see* it,” Lena says.
He opens his mouth.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 PM · I-10 EAST, PAST LORDSBURG — THE LAST LINE
body: “Sorry, I forgot how private you and Julian are. When she stars in a movie called ‘Jack’ I’ll make sure you come watch the whole thing next to me so we can see your face enjoying how authentic and humble everything is.”

He turns back around to the front. The belt lets go of his neck. His hands are shaking, both of them, and he puts them on the book on his knees to stop them, and they don’t stop, so he leaves them there and lets them shake. His heart is going like he’s run up the four flights in Delgado. He has more. There’s another one right behind that one, and one behind that, lined up and ready, every one of them true, and he sits there with them in his mouth and his teeth shut on them. The window beside him has his own face in it, faint, over the dark, and he looks past it at a fence line going by and doesn’t see the fence.
Behind Theo, Lena doesn’t say anything.

He can see a slice of her without turning, in the corner of the rearview mirror where it reaches the way-back. Her mouth opens. It shuts again. Nothing comes back up into it. Her hand goes up to the medal at her collar and closes on it and stays closed. A truck comes past the other way, high and lit, and in the light going over the inside of the van her face isn’t angry anymore, and he can’t tell what it is instead, and he doesn’t want to.

Laney’s hand comes off the back of his seat and goes to Lena’s arm, and Lena doesn’t do anything about it, either way. Laney says her name once, low, and gets nothing back. Her phone is in her lap. She turns it over, face-down, on her knee, without looking at it, and leaves her hand on top of it.
Beside him Theo takes his face out of his hands. He looks at the back of Kevin’s seat. He doesn’t try anything; there’s nothing in the bag.

Jack takes the RAZR out of his shirt pocket and opens it low on his knee, where the light of it won’t reach anybody. No bars. New Mexico has taken them. He shuts it and keeps it in his hand. In Burnaby it’s raining, eight degrees, and she has a call time in the morning, and his flannel is hanging in a wardrobe trailer across some parking lot from wherever she is tonight.

Kevin reaches out to the dash for the mix, and stops with his finger on the button, and takes the finger back. He reaches up for the map light to put it out and finds it out already, and leaves his hand up there on the switch, because there’s nothing else to do with it.
Margot drives. Both hands. Sixty-five.

It has gone cold outside. He can feel it come off the glass into his shoulder. The stars are down to the ground on every side, out here where there’s nothing to stop them, and far ahead there is one truck, two red lights, that never gets any closer.
A long way on, a sign comes up in the headlights on the right, brown and white, CONTINENTAL DIVIDE, and goes back into the dark behind them.
Nobody says anything to anybody for a hundred and fifty miles.
